quiz.why: Mercury and Venus are the only planets with no moons. Picking Mars is a common slip: Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.

quiz.p: What did Galileo see beside Jupiter in 1610?
quiz.why: He saw dots that changed sides night after night, and worked out they were moons going round Jupiter. Picking 'rings' mixes Jupiter up with Saturn, whose rings are easy to see in a telescope.

quiz.p: What is the main difference between an asteroid and a comet?
opts: An asteroid is mostly rock and metal. A comet has a lot of ice.
An asteroid is always bigger than a comet.
An asteroid goes round a planet. A comet goes round the Sun.
quiz.why: Asteroids are rocky or metal. Comets are ice, dust and rock, and their ice makes the tail near the Sun. Picking 'goes round a planet' describes a moon. Both asteroids and comets go round the Sun.

opts: Between the Earth and the Moon
quiz.why: Most asteroids go round the Sun in the asteroid belt, between Mars and Jupiter. Picking 'between the Earth and the Moon' is a fair guess, since some asteroids do pass near the Earth, but they are only a tiny few.

quiz.p: In the ice comet test, Anjali puts one dirty ice ball in the sun and one in the shade. After 30 minutes, what does the sunny one look like?
opts: Smaller, with a dark crust of dirt
Exactly the same as the shady one
quiz.why: The sun melts its ice faster. The dirt cannot melt, so it stays on the surface as a dark crust. Picking 'perfectly clean' is the guess many people make, because water usually washes dirt away.

quiz.p: Why is the nucleus of a real comet darker than coal?
opts: Its ice has turned to gas and left a crust of dark dust
It is in the Earth's shadow
quiz.why: Each pass near the Sun, ice leaves and dust stays, building a dark crust, as in the ice comet test. Picking 'burning' is a common idea, but comets do not burn. Their glow is sunlight on gas and dust.

quiz.p: A comet has passed the Sun and is now moving away from it. Where is its tail?
opts: In front of it, pointing away from the Sun
Behind it, pointing towards the Sun
It has no tail at all
quiz.why: The Sun pushes a comet's tail away from it all the time, so when the comet moves away, its tail goes in front. Picking 'behind it' is what we expect from hair or a kite, and is what happened in the fan test with the fan off.

quiz.p: What pushes a comet's tail away from the Sun?
quiz.why: Sunlight and the solar wind, a stream of tiny particles from the Sun, push the gas and dust outwards. Picking 'wind in space' is close in spirit, but space has no air, so there is no ordinary wind there.

opts: The streak of light when a bit of space rock burns up in our air
A stone that lands on the ground
A rock in the asteroid belt
quiz.why: The streak of light is the meteor. Picking 'a stone that lands' describes a meteorite, the piece that reaches the ground.

quiz.p: Why does a tiny grain glow so brightly when it enters our air?
opts: It moves so fast that it squashes the air in front of it, and the air gets extremely hot
It is on fire before it arrives
It reflects the light of the Moon
quiz.why: At tens of kilometres a second, the grain squashes the air ahead so hard that it gets hotter than a furnace. The grain turns to glowing gas. Picking 'on fire before it arrives' is a common idea, but space has no air, so nothing can burn there.

quiz.p: Why does the Geminid meteor shower come around 13 and 14 December every year?
opts: The Earth reaches the same dust trail at the same point in its path each year
The Moon sends dust in December
quiz.why: The Earth takes one year to go round the Sun, so it crosses the dust trail at the same point, on the same dates, every year. Picking 'December nights are longer' is a sensible thought, because longer nights give more time to watch, but it does not explain the dates.

quiz.p: In 1803, thousands of stones fell near L'Aigle in France. What did the scientist Jean-Baptiste Biot show?
opts: The stones really had fallen from the sky
The stones had been thrown up by a volcano
The stones had been struck by lightning
quiz.why: Biot talked to many people who saw the fall, mapped where the stones landed, and found they were unlike local rock. This convinced scientists that stones fall from space. 'Lightning' and 'volcano' were the old explanations that his study ruled out.

worksheets.title: Moons, Asteroids, Comets and Shooting Stars (core)

items.p: Match each planet to its moons.
pairs: two small moons, Phobos and Deimos
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Venus and Mercury have no moons. The giant planets have many. A strong answer could add that new small moons are still being found round the giants.

items.p: A lump of rock and metal that goes round the Sun, mostly between Mars and Jupiter, is called an ____.
items.why: Asteroids are rocky leftovers from when the planets formed.

items.p: Meena, a girl in Class 3, says: 'A shooting star is a star that falls out of the sky.' Is she right?
items.why: False. A shooting star is a grain of space dust burning up about 100 km above us. The real stars stay where they are, much, much further away.

items.p: Put these in the order they happen to one bit of space rock.
items: It lands in a field as a meteorite.
It floats in space as a meteoroid.
It glows in our air as a meteor.
a: It floats in space as a meteoroid.
It glows in our air as a meteor.
It lands in a field as a meteorite.
items.why: Meteoroid in space, meteor in the air, meteorite on the ground. A strong answer notices it is the same rock at three moments.

items.p: In the ice comet test, why did we put one ice comet in the shade?
opts: To compare it with the sunny one, so we could see what the sun changed
Because shade makes ice melt faster
items.why: The shady comet is the comparison. Everything was the same except the sun, so any difference was caused by the sun. Picking 'shade makes ice melt faster' is the opposite of what happens.

items.p: In the ice comet test, the dirt was mixed all through the ice at the start. After 30 minutes in the sun, it was a dark crust on top. Explain why.
items.a: The sun melted the ice away. The dirt could not melt, so it was left behind on the outside. The more ice went, the more dirt built up.
items.why: A strong answer says the dirt did not move up or grow. It was left behind where the ice used to be.

items.p: Draw the Sun and a comet at two places on its path: one coming in towards the Sun and one going away. Draw each comet's tail.
items.a: Both tails point straight away from the Sun. The coming-in comet has its tail behind it, and the going-away comet has its tail in front.
items.why: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun. A strong drawing shows the tail in front of the comet that is going away.
items.art: A small Sun in the middle of an empty page with a long oval path drawn round it.

items.p: Sort these into things that go round a planet and things that go round the Sun.
items: our Moon
Goes round a planet
Ceres
Goes round the Sun
Ganymede
Goes round a planet
Halley's Comet
Goes round the Sun
Phobos
Goes round a planet
the Earth
Goes round the Sun
items.a: see items
items.why: Moons go round planets. Planets, asteroids such as Ceres, and comets go round the Sun. A strong answer remembers that moons also go round the Sun, together with their planet.

items.p: Where in the sky do most shooting stars burn up?
opts: About 80 to 120 km above the ground, higher than aeroplanes
items.why: They burn up high in the air, far above aeroplanes, which fly at about 10 km. Picking 'just above the rooftops' is a common feeling, because shooting stars seem close. That is why Arjun in the story thought one landed in the next street.

items.p: Small asteroids are lumpy, like potatoes, because their gravity is too weak to pull them into a ball.
items.why: True. Big worlds pull themselves into a ball from all sides. Small asteroids do not pull hard enough, so they keep their lumpy shapes.

items.p: Arjun's grain of rava in the story could not glow on its own. What would it need to do to make a light like a shooting star?
items.a: It would have to rush into the air extremely fast, tens of kilometres every second. Then it would squash the air in front of it, which gets very hot, and the grain would turn into glowing gas.
items.why: A strong answer says it is the speed, not the size, that makes the light.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Ceres is an asteroid, going round the Sun. Io, Europa and Callisto are moons of Jupiter.

items.p: Two friends in Chennai, Kavya and Farhan, saw Comet NEOWISE in July 2020.

views.says: A comet is a lucky sign. People should make wishes when one comes.
A comet is just a lump of ice and dust that comes near the Sun on its path. It can't bring luck.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other friend has a point about.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence, such as comets returning on paths we can work out. It also gives the other side its due: Kavya is right that seeing a comet is special and makes people happy, as it did for Paati in the story. Farhan is right about what a comet is made of.
items.why: People have felt strongly about comets for thousands of years. Science tells us what a comet is, while how people feel about seeing one is their own.

items.p: Label the parts of the comet on the drawing: nucleus, coma, gas tail, dust tail, and an arrow showing the way to the Sun.
items.a: The nucleus is the small solid lump in the centre. The coma is the glowing cloud round it. The gas tail is straight and thin. The dust tail is wider and curved. Both tails point away from the arrow to the Sun.
items.why: A strong answer puts both tails on the side away from the Sun.
items.art: An unlabelled comet with a small dot in the middle, a glowing cloud, one straight thin tail and one curved wide tail, and five blank label lines.

items.p: When a solid, such as a comet's ice, turns straight into a gas without melting first, this is called ____.
items.why: In space there is no air pushing on the ice, so it turns straight into gas instead of melting into water.

items.p: In the fan test, Priya walks sideways across the fan's air with her paper comet. Where does the tail point?
opts: Away from the fan, not behind her hand
items.why: The fan's air pushes the tail away from the fan, whichever way she walks. Picking 'behind her hand' is what happened with the fan off.

items.p: With the fan off, the paper comet's tail trailed behind. With the fan on, it pointed away from the fan. What does this tell you about real comets and the Sun?
items.a: A comet's tail is not made by the comet moving. It is pushed by the Sun. So a real comet's tail points away from the Sun, even when the comet is moving away from the Sun.
items.why: A strong answer compares the two parts of the test and links the fan to the Sun's push.

items.p: The fan in the fan test is just like the Sun, because both push in one direction only.
items.why: False. A fan blows one way. The Sun pushes out in every direction, so a comet's tail points away from the Sun wherever the comet is. A strong answer says how the model and the real thing differ.

items.p: Ganymede is wider than the planet Mercury. So why is Ganymede called a moon and not a planet?
items.a: Because Ganymede goes round Jupiter, not round the Sun on its own path. A moon is named by what it goes round, not by how big it is.
items.why: A strong answer says 'moon' means a world that goes round a planet.

items.p: Lonar Lake in Maharashtra is round, with steep sides. How did the hollow it sits in form?
opts: A meteorite hit the ground very fast and blasted out a crater
An elephant herd stamped the ground flat
items.why: Lonar Lake fills a crater made by a meteorite impact long ago. Picking 'people dug it' is reasonable for many Indian tanks and ponds, but not for a hollow this big and this round.

items.p: Put these in order, from the smallest to the biggest.
items: Phobos, a moon of Mars, about 22 km
a grain that makes a shooting star
Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter
Ceres, the biggest asteroid, about 940 km
a: a grain that makes a shooting star
Phobos, a moon of Mars, about 22 km
Ceres, the biggest asteroid, about 940 km
items.why: A grain is smaller than a millimetre. Phobos is about 22 km, Ceres about 940 km, and Ganymede about 5,300 km. A strong answer notices that a moon can be smaller than an asteroid.

items.p: Two scientists disagree about where the Earth's seas came from.

views.says: The young Earth was very hot and may have lost its first water. Comets and icy asteroids crashing into it brought much of the water back.
Water in many comets is slightly different from sea water. Most of the Earth's water was there from the start, inside its rocks.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other scientist has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the evidence each scientist gives. Dr Meenakshi is right that comets hold lots of ice. Dr Rupa is right that the water in many comets does not quite match our seas. Real scientists still argue about this, and the answer may be a bit of both.
items.why: This is a real, open question. Both views have evidence.

items.p: Nila counted 7 shooting stars from her city terrace. Her cousin in a village far from any town counted more than 50 on the same night. Why?
opts: The village sky was darker, so faint meteors showed up
More dust fell on the village
items.why: The same shower falls over the whole area, but city lights hide the faint meteors. Picking 'more dust fell on the village' is a good thought, but both places were under the same shower.

items.p: Halley's Comet came near the Sun in 1986 and will come again in 2061. Will it look exactly the same? Explain.
items.a: Not exactly. Each time it passes the Sun, it loses some ice and dust, so it is a little smaller, with a little more dark crust. Its brightness also depends on where the Earth is when it passes.
items.why: A strong answer uses what happened to the ice comet: each pass near the Sun takes some of it away.

items.p: Draw the Earth's round path and a comet's long, stretched path crossing it. Show where the comet's dust is, and where the Earth will see a meteor shower.
items.a: A circle for the Earth's path, a long oval for the comet's path crossing it, dots of dust along the oval, and a mark at the crossing for the meteor shower.
items.why: A strong drawing puts dust along the whole comet path, not just near the comet, and marks the crossing.
items.art: A small Sun in the middle of an empty page.

items.p: Match each moon to something true about it.
pairs: has an ocean under its ice
has thick air and lakes of a liquid called methane
is the biggest moon in the solar system
is a small, lumpy moon of Mars
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each moon is a different kind of world. A strong answer notices that moons are as different from each other as planets are.

items.p: A night when many shooting stars come from the same part of the sky is called a meteor ____.
items.why: A meteor shower happens when the Earth passes through a trail of dust left by a comet or an asteroid.

items.p: Sort these into what makes a shooting star and what does not.
items: a grain of dust rushing into our air
Makes a shooting star
a star moving across the sky
Does not
a pebble-sized rock rushing into our air
Makes a shooting star
an aeroplane's lights
Does not
a satellite catching sunlight
Does not
items.a: see items
items.why: Only bits of space rock rushing into our air make meteors. Satellites and aeroplanes move steadily across the sky for many seconds, while a meteor lasts about a second.

items.p: A grain the size of a grain of rava can make a shooting star, but it does not leave a meteorite on the ground.
items.why: True. Such a small grain burns up completely, high in the air. Only bigger pieces leave something to land.

items.p: Label the planets and the asteroid belt on the drawing: Mars, the asteroid belt, Jupiter, and Jupiter's four big moons.
items.a: Mars is the small planet nearer the Sun. The asteroid belt is the ring of dots beyond Mars. Jupiter is the big planet beyond the belt, with four small dots beside it for Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
items.why: A strong answer puts the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

worksheets.title: Comets That Fade and Rocks That Arrive (challenge)

items.p: A comet loses some ice every time it passes the Sun. What will happen to a comet after thousands of passes? What might be left?
items.a: It will run out of ice. Then it can stop growing a tail, and may be left as a dark, dusty, rocky lump, a bit like an asteroid. Or it may crumble into a trail of dust.
items.why: A strong answer uses the ice comet test: ice leaves, dirt stays. It may also say some objects, like Phaethon, sit between a comet and an asteroid.

items.p: Three people talk about what to call Phaethon, the parent of the Geminid shower. Phaethon is rocky, but near the Sun it sheds dust.

views.says: Phaethon is an asteroid, because it is rock and has no icy tail.
Phaethon behaves like a comet, because it sheds dust near the Sun and makes a meteor shower.
Maybe Phaethon is an old comet that has lost all its ice.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say what the others have right.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence about what Phaethon is made of and what it does. Tanvi is right that it is rocky. Lakshmi is right that it acts a bit like a comet. Ishita's idea is one that some scientists also take seriously. It shows that nature does not always fit our boxes.
items.why: Phaethon really is hard to name. The words 'asteroid' and 'comet' are boxes people made, and some objects sit between them.

items.p: Swathi watches the Geminids on 13 December and sees many shooting stars. She watches again on 25 December and sees almost none. Explain why.
items.a: By 25 December, the Earth has moved on along its path and passed out of Phaethon's dust trail. There is little dust left for it to run into.
items.why: A strong answer links the dates to where the Earth is on its path round the Sun.

items.p: Anu wants to repeat the ice comet test to find out if more dirt makes a darker crust. Which test is fair?
opts: Two ice comets, one with 1 spoon of dirt and one with 3 spoons, both in the sun
Two ice comets with 1 spoon of dirt, one in the sun and one in the shade
One ice comet with 3 spoons of dirt in the sun, and one with no dirt in the shade
items.why: To test the amount of dirt, change only the dirt and keep everything else the same, including the place. The last choice changes two things at once, so you could not tell which one made the difference.

items.p: A spacecraft coming back from space to Earth gets very hot on the outside. How is this like a shooting star?
items.a: Both rush into the air very fast and squash the air in front of them, which gets very hot. The shooting star's grain burns up, but the spacecraft has a heat shield that protects it.
items.why: A strong answer names squashed air as the cause of the heat in both.

items.p: A comet glows near the Sun because it is on fire.
items.why: False. There is no air in space, so nothing burns there. The gas and dust round the comet shine in sunlight, and the gas also gives out a glow of its own because sunlight energises it.

items.p: Draw a comet at three places on its path: far out, coming close to the Sun, and nearest the Sun. Show how its tail changes.
items.a: Far out: a small dark lump, no tail. Coming close: a small coma and a short tail. Nearest the Sun: a big coma and a long tail. Every tail points away from the Sun.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the tail growing as the comet nears the Sun and always pointing away from it.
items.art: A Sun at the left edge and a long empty oval path stretching to the right.

items.p: Saturn is smaller than Jupiter, but Saturn has more known moons. What does this tell you?
opts: A bigger planet does not always have more moons
Saturn is really bigger than Jupiter
items.why: Size is not the only thing that sets how many moons a planet has. Also, many small moons are still being found, so the counts keep changing. Picking 'moon counts never change' is wrong: dozens of new small moons have been found in recent years.

items.p: Galileo's dots sometimes disappeared for a night. Give two reasons a moon of Jupiter might not be seen.
items.a: It could be behind Jupiter, so Jupiter hides it. It could be in front of Jupiter, so it is lost against Jupiter's bright face. It could also be in Jupiter's shadow.
items.why: A strong answer thinks about where the moon is on its path when seen from the side, as in the buttons-round-the-plate activity.

items.p: Put these events from the story of meteorites in the order they happened.
items: Biot studies the stones that fell at L'Aigle.
Chladni writes that fireballs come from space.
Scientists say stones can't fall from the sky.
Scientists accept that stones fall from space.
a: Scientists say stones can't fall from the sky.
Chladni writes that fireballs come from space.
Biot studies the stones that fell at L'Aigle.
Scientists accept that stones fall from space.
items.why: Chladni's book came in 1794 and the L'Aigle fall in 1803. A strong answer notices that careful evidence, not just an idea, changed people's minds.

items.p: The Earth gains thousands of tonnes of space dust each year. Does this make the Earth heavier? What else might it lose?
items.a: Yes, the dust adds a little. But the Earth also loses a little, because the lightest gases, hydrogen and helium, slowly escape from the top of its air into space.
items.why: A strong answer thinks about what comes in and what goes out, not just one side. Scientists think the Earth loses about as much as, or a little more than, it gains.

items.p: Why do scientists search for meteorites on the ice in Antarctica?
opts: Dark stones are easy to spot on white ice, where no other rocks are lying about
More meteorites fall there than anywhere else
Meteorites are attracted to cold places
It is the closest place to space
items.why: Meteorites fall all over the Earth, but on the ice almost any dark stone you find came from above. Picking 'more fall there' is a fair guess, but it is about finding them, not about how many fall.

items.p: The stream of tiny particles that flows out from the Sun and pushes a comet's gas tail is called the solar ____.
items.why: The solar wind is not air. It is a stream of tiny charged particles from the Sun.

items.p: Label the moments in the life of one bit of comet dust: it leaves the comet, it drifts along the comet's path, it meets the Earth, it glows as a meteor.
items.a: The dust leaves the comet near the Sun, drifts along the comet's oval path, is met by the Earth where the paths cross, and glows as a meteor high in our air.
items.why: A strong answer shows the whole journey in order and puts the meteor where the two paths cross.
items.art: A diagram with a Sun, a comet on a long oval path, the Earth on a circle crossing the oval, and four blank label lines along the way.

items.p: Two people argue about whether we should spend money to push dangerous asteroids off course.

views.says: Yes. A big hit is rare, but it could be terrible. The DART test in 2022 showed that it can be done.

views.who: Sana, who runs a school in a village
views.says: No. A big hit is very unlikely in our lifetime. The money could help children today.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer weighs how rare a big hit is against how bad it would be. Dr Lakshmi is right that being ready matters. Sana is right that money spent here is not spent elsewhere.
items.why: This is a real choice about risk. There is no single right answer.

applications: Space agencies track asteroids that come near the Earth, so any danger is known years ahead.
In 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft crashed into a small asteroid and changed its path, as a test of how to protect the Earth.
Spacecraft bring back bits of asteroids and comets, such as Japan's Hayabusa2 from the asteroid Ryugu, to learn what the early solar system was made of.
Engineers put shields on spacecraft and the International Space Station to protect them from tiny grains of space dust.
Heat shields on spacecraft coming back to Earth work against the same squashed, hot air that makes shooting stars glow.
Meteor cameras around the world record fireballs and work out where any meteorites landed, so people can find them.

open_questions.q: Is there life in the ocean under the ice of Jupiter's moon Europa?
open_questions.why_open: Europa very likely has a salty ocean, but nobody has looked inside it yet. NASA's Europa Clipper spacecraft is on its way to study it.

open_questions.q: Where did the Earth's water come from?
open_questions.why_open: Some was probably there from the start, and some may have come from comets and asteroids. Scientists still argue about how much came from each.

open_questions.q: How exactly did our Moon form?
open_questions.why_open: Most scientists think a giant crash made it, but no computer model yet matches every fact about Moon rock.

open_questions.q: Exactly how much space dust reaches the Earth each day?
open_questions.why_open: Different ways of measuring give very different answers, from a few tonnes to many tonnes a day.

maths.problem: A grain that makes a shooting star moves about 30 kilometres every second. How far does it go in 10 seconds?
maths.explain: Each second it goes 30 km. In 10 seconds it goes 10 times as far. 30 times 10 is 300. So it goes 300 km, about the distance from Chennai to Bengaluru.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how fast a grain really goes, which is what makes it glow.
maths.context: This is about how fast the grains that make shooting stars move. You met this in the grain of rava activity.

maths.problem: In a made-up ice comet test, the sunny comet went from 4 cm to 2.5 cm tall in 30 minutes. The shady comet went from 4 cm to 3.5 cm. How much did each one shrink? How many times as much did the sunny one shrink?
maths.answer: The sunny one shrank 1.5 cm and the shady one 0.5 cm. The sunny one shrank 3 times as much.
maths.explain: 4 take away 2.5 is 1.5. 4 take away 3.5 is 0.5. 1.5 is three lots of 0.5. So the sunny comet shrank 3 times as much.
maths.why_maths: Taking away the end height from the start height shows exactly how much each comet lost, so we can compare them fairly.
maths.context: This is about the ice comet test, where one dirty ice ball sat in the sun and one in the shade.

maths.problem: Halley's Comet came near the Sun in 1986. It comes back about every 75 years. In which year will it come back? If you were born in 2017, how old will you be then?
maths.explain: 1986 plus 75 is 2061. 2061 take away 2017 is 44. The real time between visits changes by a year or two, because the planets' gravity tugs on the comet.
maths.why_maths: Adding the years between visits tells us when a comet will return, which is how astronomers plan to watch for it.
maths.context: This is about Halley's Comet, which Paati saw in 1986 in the story.

maths.problem: In a made-up Geminid watch, Kavya counted 2 shooting stars in the first 10 minutes, 3 in the next 10 minutes and 5 in the last 10 minutes. Draw a bar chart. How many did she see in all? What pattern do you see?
maths.answer: 10 in all. The count went up as the night went on.
maths.explain: 2 plus 3 plus 5 is 10. The bars get taller, so more shooting stars came later. The Geminids' part of the sky climbs higher as the night goes on, so more meteors can reach your view.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance when most shooting stars came, which helps you choose the best time to watch.
maths.context: This is about the shooting star watch, where you count meteors every 10 minutes.

chart.title: Made-up example: shooting stars every 10 minutes

maths.problem: The Earth has 1 moon, Mars has 2 and Neptune has 16. Jupiter has more than 90, and Saturn has more than 270, though Saturn is smaller than Jupiter. Put the five planets in order of how many moons they have. Does the biggest planet have the most moons?
maths.answer: Earth, Mars, Neptune, Jupiter, Saturn. No. Jupiter is biggest, but Saturn has the most known moons.
maths.explain: 1 is less than 2, 2 is less than 16, 16 is less than 90, and 90 is less than 270. Jupiter is the biggest planet, but Saturn has more moons. So size alone does not set the number of moons.
maths.why_maths: Ordering the numbers lets us test an idea, 'bigger planets have more moons', and see where it breaks.
maths.context: This is about the moons of the planets, from the card on moons.

maths.problem: The Earth takes about 365 days to go round the Sun. The Geminids peak around 14 December this year. About when will they peak next year? Why?
maths.explain: After 365 days, the Earth is back at the same point on its path, where it crosses Phaethon's dust trail. So the shower comes back on about the same date.
maths.why_maths: Knowing that a year is one trip round the Sun lets you use the calendar to predict meteor showers.
maths.context: This is about meteor showers, which come on the same dates every year.

roots.context: We have learned about moons, asteroids, comets and shooting stars. Now we ask what a comet's journey tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your sunny ice comet shrank fastest, and its dirt stayed behind as a dark crust and a muddy trail. A real comet near the Sun loses ice and dust in the same way. The Earth runs into the dust that comets leave along their paths. So many shooting stars are tiny pieces of comets, ending their journey in our air.
deep_truth.habit: We give a comet, its tail, a shooting star and dust on a roof four different names, as if they were four different things. They are the same ice, rock and dust at different moments of one journey.
deep_truth.evidence: In the ice comet test, the comet in the sun lost ice fastest and left its dirt behind, on top and in the plate. Real comets get dark crusts and leave dust along their paths. Meteor showers come on the dates the Earth crosses those dust trails.

three.who_am_i: Every atom in your body was once in the cloud of gas and dust that made the Sun, the planets and the comets.
three.what_is_life: Living things are made mostly of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen. Comets are full of these too.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth is still being added to. Space dust falls on it every day, even on your balcony.

roots.thread: Before the planets, there was one spinning cloud of gas and dust round the young Sun. Out of it came the Sun, the planets, the moons, the asteroids and the comets. They have different names, but they are made from the same cloud. Comets still carry some of that first ice and dust. Near the Sun they lose it, and some of it falls on the Earth as shooting stars. So the pieces of the one cloud are still meeting each other again.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu: by knowing one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. A pot or a cup is a name given to a new shape. What is real is the clay.
teachings.link: Comet, tail, meteor and space dust are names for one material at different moments, as pot and cup are names for clay in different shapes.

teachings.teaching: Everything that is put together changes and does not last. A person who sees this clearly suffers less.
teachings.link: A comet loses some of itself every time it passes the Sun, like your ice comet in the sunny window. In the end, its ice runs out.

teachings.teaching: On those who step into the same rivers, different and again different waters flow.
teachings.link: Halley's Comet keeps its name and its path, but each time it returns it has lost some ice and dust. It is the same comet and not quite the same.

science.text: Meteor showers happen when the Earth passes through dust left along the paths of comets. Schiaparelli linked the Perseids to comet Swift-Tuttle in 1866.
Some of the Earth's water may have come from comets and asteroids. How much is still argued about.

other_view.who: The Nyaya and Vaisheshika schools of Indian philosophy
other_view.view: When parts come together, they make a real new whole, not just a name. A pot is a real pot, not only clay. In the same way, a comet is a real comet while it lasts, and a meteor is a real meteor, even if they share the same dust.

practice.title: Watch a drop leave
practice.say: Let's put an ice cube on a steel plate and sit very still. Watch one drop form at the bottom of the ice. Breathe in slowly. As the drop runs away, breathe out slowly. Let's do this for five drops. The ice is getting smaller, and the water is going somewhere new. Where will it go next?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. The ice comet uses crushed ice, because muddy water left to freeze lets the soil sink to the bottom, and the comet would then be clean on top. Used tea leaves are added because they cling to the ice and make the crust easy to see. Homes with no direct sun use a plate on a vessel of warm tap water instead. The shady comet still melts slowly in an Indian room, and the parent note says so: in space, far from the Sun, a comet would not change at all. The fan test asks for slow walking, because a fast walk beats the fan's air and the tail flops. The Geminid watch is outside the spine, needs a grown-up on the terrace, and says honestly that a city sky may show only a few meteors an hour. The magnet dust hunt says plainly that most magnetic grains in city dust are not from space. The Jupiter project needs binoculars, bought or borrowed, and Jupiter in the evening sky, so it is outside the spine. Both games work for one child with a parent. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, most scientists in Europe did not believe that stones could fall from the sky. Farmers told of hot stones landing in their fields after a bright flash and a bang. Learned men said these were mistakes. The stones, they said, had been struck by lightning or thrown out of volcanoes, and fireballs were a kind of weather high in the air. In 1794, the German scientist Ernst Chladni wrote a book saying the opposite. Fireballs, he said, were lumps of rock and iron coming in from space, glowing as they rushed through the air. Many scientists laughed at him. Then, on 26 April 1803, thousands of stones fell around the town of L'Aigle in France. The young scientist Jean-Baptiste Biot was sent to find out what had happened. He visited many villages, talked to the people who had seen and heard the fall, and collected stones. He mapped where they had landed, in an oval area several kilometres long. The stones were unlike any rock found nearby. After his report, scientists accepted that stones really do fall from space. Today we call them meteorites.
how_we_found_out.who: Ernst Chladni, a German scientist, and Jean-Baptiste Biot, a French scientist
how_we_found_out.when: 1794 (Chladni's book) and 1803 (the fall at L'Aigle and Biot's report)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Most scientists thought stones could not fall from the sky, and that fireballs were a kind of weather. Biot's careful study of the L'Aigle fall showed that the stones came from space.
